source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test); the engine has no initial-risk accessor beyond ctx.EntryPrice(), so every risk-multiple candidate introduces a stopDistance parameter standing in for the actual initial stop distance and notes the mismatch risk if the real entry-side stop differs

candidates.name: InitialStopAtrMultiple
candidates.quote: it would be very unusual to set an initial stop that is less than two Average True Ranges (ATRs) from the current price, and the initial stop may sometimes be more than four ATRs away from the current price
candidates.description: Initial protective stop is placed a multiple of ATR beyond the entry price; the ATR is captured once at entry and the stop level is then fixed for the life of the trade.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order beyond the ATR-derived level; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: needs an ATR and the ATR must be captured once at entry and held constant, not recomputed every bar

notes: Grimes also mentions an equivalent N-times-average-daily-range or N-times-one-day-stdev volatility stop; treat as the same family with a different volatility measure.
atrLength not given for this stop specifically; defaulted to 20 to match Grimes's Keltner/EMA convention elsewhere in the book.

candidates.name: StopBeyondPenultimateSwingPoint
candidates.quote: you do not want to see the market take out the closest pivot low ... It is also possible to step back to the penultimate pivot in many cases ... but with the trade-off of a much smaller position size
candidates.description: Initial stop is placed beyond the second-most-recent (penultimate) confirmed swing low rather than the nearest one, for a wider, lower-probability-of-being-hit stop.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order beyond the penultimate pivot; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection at a rank deeper than the most recent confirmed pivot

notes: This is InitialStopBeyondSwingAtEntry with a pivot-rank parameter; the rank-1 case (nearest pivot) is presumably already the existing rule.

candidates.name: StopBeyondConsolidationExtreme
candidates.quote: If buying against a sloppy support area with many shadows below, the only stop that makes sense is beyond the most extreme low
candidates.description: When buying against a messy support area, the initial stop is placed beyond the single lowest low of the recent consolidation lookback, not just beyond the nearest pivot.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order beyond the most extreme low; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: a lowest-low window over N bars plus an ATR buffer

notes: consolLookback and stopBuffer are not numbered by Grimes; defaults chosen to match StopBeyondRecentRangeExtreme's existing convention.

candidates.name: ReenterBeyondNewExtremeAfterStopOut
candidates.quote: If this happens and you are stopped out of the position on a fakeout, it is necessary to rebuy with a new stop beyond the new, lowest extreme
candidates.description: After being stopped out on a dip below support that then reverses (a fakeout), re-enter long with a new stop placed beyond the new, lower extreme that was just made.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() == 0 and ctx.BarsSinceExit() <= reentryBars and not ctx.LastTradeWasWinner() and close[0] > low[1]
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop re-entry after the reversal is confirmed; mechanized as close-then-next-open

complexity.reason: reads recent trade-history accessors (BarsSinceExit, last-trade outcome) plus a same-bar reversal test

notes: Close cousin of ReenterAfterQuickStopOut / StopRunReclaimReentry; the new stop this candidate implies is G08-03 applied again at the new extreme.

candidates.name: ProfitTargetAtOneRiskMultiplePartial
candidates.quote: I usually exit between 25 and 33 percent of the position on a limit order at a profit equal to my initial risk in the trade
candidates.description: A fraction of the position is taken off at a limit price equal to one initial-risk multiple of profit above the entry.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at entry + 1x risk, working GTC; mechanized as a stop-level test on the bar's extreme

complexity.reason: requires a stopDistance parameter standing in for the actual initial risk, which the engine cannot read back from the entry-side stop rule

notes: The generator's Exit rules likely cannot express a partial-percentage exit natively; exitFraction is recorded for the authoring pass to decide whether to model as a full exit at this level (a simplification) or leave partial sizing out of scope.
stopDistance should mirror whatever the paired Entry/Exit stop rule (e.g. G08-01 or G08-03) uses, or the risk multiple will be inconsistent with the actual initial stop.

candidates.name: ProfitTargetAtTwoRiskMultiplesPartial
candidates.quote: I also make it a point to be down to between one-third to half my initial size at two times my initial risk, and then manage the remainder according to a different set of rules
candidates.description: A second tranche is taken off (leaving roughly one-third to one-half of the original size) at a limit price equal to two initial-risk multiples of profit above the entry.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at entry + 2x risk, working GTC; mechanized as a stop-level test on the bar's extreme

complexity.reason: same stopDistance-parameter caveat as G08-05

notes: Same parameterized rule as G08-05 with riskMultiple=2; kept as a separate candidate because Grimes treats the two tranches as distinct decision points with different downstream management.

candidates.name: TightenStopAfterOneRiskMultipleReached
candidates.quote: When the market reaches $52.50, it may make sense to tighten the stop to just under your entry point or even higher
candidates.description: Once the open trade has moved one initial-risk multiple into profit, tighten the protective stop to just under (long) the entry price.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.OpenPositionProfit() > 0 and high[0] >= ctx.EntryPrice() + riskMultiple * stopDistance ; then close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() - tightenBuffer
candidates.book_order_type: mental/manual stop adjustment; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: cross-bar state: once armed by the 1x move, the tightened stop level must persist

notes: Grimes leaves the exact tightened level to discretion ("or even higher"); tightenBuffer=0 (exact breakeven) is the conservative default chosen for this candidate.

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAfterTwoRiskMultiplesReached
candidates.quote: Once this profit target is hit, it usually makes sense to tighten the stop on the remainder of the trade to the entry price, essentially working a breakeven stop on the rest of the trade
candidates.description: After the 2x-initial-risk profit target has been reached (and part of the position taken off there), move the stop on the remainder to exactly the entry price.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MaxPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * stopDistance ; then close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice()
candidates.book_order_type: mental/manual stop adjustment; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: arms on a peak-profit accessor, then holds a fixed level

notes: This is essentially BreakevenStop with activationProfit expressed as a risk multiple (2x stopDistance) instead of a flat dollar amount.

candidates.name: SwingLowTrailingStopInTrend
candidates.quote: in an uptrend, a tight stop could be trailed under the highest pivot low of the trend. Slightly wider stops could go under the second-highest pivot low, probably working both of these stops on a close-only basis
candidates.description: In a trend, trail the protective stop under the most recent confirmed swing low (tight variant) or under the second-most-recent swing low (wider variant), checked on closes only.
candidates.book_order_type: close-only stop, no intrabar trigger

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, re-read every bar

notes: swingRank=2 gives the looser, second-highest-pivot-low variant Grimes also describes.

candidates.name: TightenStopUnderPriorBarExtremeInParabolicRun
candidates.quote: A trader holding a long position in a runaway trend like this could have worked a stop each day below the previous day's lows
candidates.description: During a sharp, parabolic momentum run, use a very tight trailing stop set just below the previous bar's low, deliberately courting an early exit to lock in the blow-off gains.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order at previous bar's extreme; mechanized as close-based since intrabar stops are not modelled

complexity.reason: a bare comparison against the previous bar's low

notes: Grimes ties this specifically to a parabolic/runaway-trend context; without a parabolic-context gate this degenerates to a universal one-bar trail, which is much more aggressive than intended. Consider gating on a large-recent-range or consecutive-strong-bar filter.

candidates.name: ChandelierAtrTrailFromTrendExtreme
candidates.quote: Chuck LeBeau's chandelier stop, which basically hangs a stop a fixed number of ATRs from the extreme point of a trend, creating a stop level that is conceptually similar to the Parabolic without the acceleration factor
candidates.description: Trail the stop a fixed multiple of ATR below the highest high made since entry (long), with no acceleration factor (unlike the Parabolic).
candidates.book_order_type: stop order below the chandelier level; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: needs the running highest-high since entry plus an ATR

notes: AtrTrailingStop trails from peak dollar profit; this candidate trails from the peak PRICE since entry, which is closer to LeBeau's original chandelier definition and may already be equivalent depending on how AtrTrailingStop computes its peak.

candidates.name: ParabolicSarTrailingStop
candidates.quote: It works by identifying the most extreme trend point (highest point in an uptrend or lowest point in a downtrend), and then placing a stop a certain distance from that extreme point. Each day, the stop is moved closer to that extreme point by an amount called the acceleration factor
candidates.description: Wilder's Parabolic SAR trailing stop: the stop starts at the extreme point of the trend and is ratcheted toward price each bar by an acceleration factor that itself increases as the trend extends, used here only as an exit-and-flatten tool (not a reverse-and-flip system).
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] <= sar[0]  // sar[0] = sar[1] + af[1] * (extremePoint[1] - sar[1]), af ratchets from afStart toward afMax by afStep on each new extreme
candidates.book_order_type: stop-and-reverse originally, mechanized here as an exit-only stop, close-based

complexity.reason: a recursive, self-accelerating state variable carried across every bar since the trend began, plus extreme-point tracking

notes: ParabolicAccelerationExit in the catalog compares two successive leg magnitudes, which is a different mechanism from Wilder's actual SAR recursion; this candidate is the literal SAR formula and is likely a genuinely new rule despite the name overlap.

candidates.name: TrailingStopFirstOppositeClose
candidates.quote: a simple plan might be to stop out of an uptrending market on the first down close
candidates.description: Exit a long trend position on the very first close that is lower than the prior close.
candidates.book_order_type: market exit on close; mechanized as close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: a bare one-bar close comparison

notes: Grimes explicitly flags this family as statistically naive (three-down-closes is usually primed for a bounce), so record but flag confidence medium-low on it being a good rule; still a valid mechanical candidate.

candidates.name: TrailingStopLowestLowNBarsAgo
candidates.quote: a simple plan might be to stop out of an uptrending market on the first down close, at the lowest low of three days ago, or on two consecutive downward closes
candidates.description: Trailing stop set at the low of a fixed number of bars back (Grimes's example: three bars ago).
candidates.book_order_type: stop order at a fixed lookback bar's low; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: a bare fixed-offset comparison

notes: Ambiguous phrasing: could mean the low of the bar exactly N bars back (as coded) or the lowest low over the last N bars (a Donchian floor, which would duplicate StopBeyondRecentRangeExtreme more directly); flagged for the authoring pass to pick.

candidates.name: TrailingStopTwoConsecutiveOppositeCloses
candidates.quote: a simple plan might be to stop out of an uptrending market on the first down close, at the lowest low of three days ago, or on two consecutive downward closes
candidates.description: Exit a long trend position after two consecutive closes each lower than the one before.
candidates.book_order_type: market exit on close; mechanized as close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: a bare two-bar close comparison

notes: Very close to the existing ConsecutiveCloseExit; kept for completeness since Grimes states it as a distinct trailing-stop option.

candidates.name: TrailingStopAtrMultipleFromPriorBarExtreme
candidates.quote: also consider stops that limit your loss on any one day, perhaps stopping out a certain ATR multiple from the previous day's high, low, or closing values
candidates.description: Trailing stop set a fixed ATR multiple away from the previous bar's high, low, or close (trader's choice of reference).
candidates.book_order_type: stop order offset from the previous bar's extreme; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: a fixed-offset comparison plus an ATR window

notes: refPrice selects which of the prior bar's high/low/close is the anchor; Grimes leaves the choice open.

candidates.name: TrendLineBreakStopRequiresConfirmation
candidates.quote: If you want to use a trend line as a trailing stop, it might make sense to require significant price action under the trend line ... multiple closes, consolidation under, multiple legs under
candidates.description: Only treat a trend-line break as a stop-out once price has closed below the projected trend line on multiple (not just one) consecutive bars.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] < trendLine(0) and close[1] < trendLine(1) and ... for confirmCloses consecutive bars
candidates.book_order_type: close-based exit, requiring confirmation over several bars

complexity.reason: needs trend-line projection from swing pivots plus a persistent multi-bar confirmation counter

notes: Grimes leaves the exact confirmation rule (closes vs. consolidation vs. legs) undefined; confirmCloses=2 is a reasonable default for the closes variant.

candidates.name: MovingAverageCloseBelowExit
candidates.quote: Many traders will get into a trending trade and will then stop out when price touches or, in some cases, closes below a moving average
candidates.description: Exit a long trend trade when the close crosses below (or the bar merely touches) a chosen moving average.
candidates.book_order_type: close-based moving-average stop

complexity.reason: needs a moving average

notes: Grimes explicitly says the MA length choice (100/50/20) is arbitrary; 20 chosen as default to match Keltner-family conventions elsewhere. A touch-only (not close-only) variant would compare low[0] instead of close[0].

candidates.name: TimeStopNoProfitWithinWindow
candidates.quote: if a trade does not hit some kind of predetermined profit limit within a certain time, the trade will be exited after that time window expires
candidates.description: If a trade has not reached its profit target within N bars of entry, exit at market.
candidates.book_order_type: market exit once the window expires

complexity.reason: cross-bar state: bars-since-entry counter plus a profit gate

notes: Grimes gives no specific bar count or profit threshold for this general rule; defaults are placeholders. profitThreshold=0 makes this close to the existing NumBarsIfLosing at numBars=maxBars.

candidates.name: TimeStopProgressiveTightening
candidates.quote: tighten the stop very close to current market prices, moving it closer as time goes on in a similar fashion to the movement of the Parabolic SAR's stop levels
candidates.description: Instead of a hard exit at the time-stop deadline, progressively tighten the stop toward the current market price as bars elapse since entry, so open risk shrinks continuously through the time window.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() + (close[0] - ctx.EntryPrice()) * (1 - ctx.BarsSinceEntry() / maxBars)  // stop tightens linearly toward price as BarsSinceEntry -> maxBars
candidates.book_order_type: manually ratcheted stop, tightened bar by bar

complexity.reason: Grimes gives no formula for the tightening rate, only an analogy to the Parabolic; a design decision (linear vs. accelerating) is needed before coding

notes: The pseudocode's linear interpolation is one reasonable design choice among several; flagged research because the book does not specify the tightening curve.

candidates.name: StopWidensToEmergingSwingStructure
candidates.quote: When emerging market structure suggests the need for a slightly wider stop ... the stop must remain inside the initial 1 x risk parameter; this is a hard limit established at the time of trade entry that can never be violated
candidates.description: The initial stop may be widened, but only up to the original 1x-risk boundary, when a new swing point forms that redefines the market structure the stop is protecting.
candidates.pseudocode: newStop = min(originalStopLevel_relaxedUp, ctx.EntryPrice() - 1 * stopDistance)  // long: newStop cannot go below entry - 1*stopDistance
candidates.book_order_type: manual stop revision, capped at the original 1x risk envelope

complexity.reason: "emerging market structure" is not defined precisely enough to code without a design decision on which new swing event triggers the widening

notes: Really a modifier on whichever initial-stop rule (G08-01/G08-02/G08-03) is in play, not a standalone exit; recorded separately because Grimes calls it out as a distinct, rare, bounded exception to the never-widen rule.

candidates.name: GapAgainstPositionRecoveryHold
candidates.quote: if you are holding a long position that gaps down and immediately starts trading up, it may make sense to set a new stop under the day's low to give the market a chance at recovery
candidates.description: If a long position gaps down at the open but the session immediately trades back up from the open, replace the stop with one placed under the session's low so far, rather than exiting at the gap.
candidates.pseudocode: open[0] < close[1] and close[0] > open[0] ; then close[0] <= sessionLow(0)
candidates.book_order_type: revised stop under the session low; mechanized as close-based

complexity.reason: needs a running session-low accessor (lowest low since session open) plus a same-bar recovery test

notes: Session-low-so-far is approximated as lowest(low, barsSinceSessionOpen); needs the corpus's session-boundary helpers.

candidates.name: GapAgainstPositionPressesLowerExit
candidates.quote: if the market opens down and immediately presses lower, or breaks lower out of an opening range, there is a good chance that it could trend down all day. Long positions should be dumped immediately
candidates.description: If a long position gaps down at the open and the market then breaks below the opening range low, exit immediately rather than waiting for the original stop.
candidates.book_order_type: market exit; mechanized as close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: needs an opening-range low accessor

notes: Companion to G08-22: same gap-down setup, opposite continuation, opposite management decision.

candidates.name: LimitExitInsideSwingPivotOffset
candidates.quote: you would place a limit to buy above $10.00 ... and a limit to sell somewhere below $20.00 ... It rarely makes sense to put your orders on the other side of a visible chart point
candidates.description: A profit-taking limit order at a visible market-structure point (swing pivot) is placed a small offset inside the pivot rather than exactly at or beyond it, since the level may not trade through.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order placed inside the visible pivot; mechanized as a bar-extreme test

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection

notes: SwingPivotTarget already has a toleranceAtr parameter that appears to implement exactly this inside-the-pivot offset.

candidates.name: ProfitTargetCappedAtNearestSwingPivot
candidates.quote: If you normally take profits at risk multiples and find yourself entering an order to buy or sell beyond one of these visible points, it probably makes sense to tighten the orders up a little bit and bring them inside the swings
candidates.description: When a risk-multiple profit target would fall beyond the nearest visible swing pivot, use the (tighter) swing-pivot-inside offset instead of the risk-multiple level.
candidates.pseudocode: targetLevel = min(ctx.EntryPrice() + riskMultiple * stopDistance, swingHigh(pivotIndex, swingStrength) - offsetTicks * ctx.MinMove()) ; high[0] >= targetLevel
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the tighter of the two levels

complexity.reason: composes a risk-multiple target with swing-pivot detection and takes the minimum of the two

notes: A refinement rule layering G08-05/06's risk-multiple target with G08-24's pivot-offset target; the authoring pass may prefer to keep these as two independent Exit rules ORed together rather than one composite, since the pane system already ORs exits.

candidates.name: CloseInSessionRangeExtremeDecile
candidates.quote: Calculate the close as percent of day's range = [(last print - day's low)/day's range] x 100 ... color code the entire indicator red for any values where close as percent of day's range <= 20, and green if >= 80
candidates.description: Flags when the current close sits in the bottom or top decile-scale fraction of the session's range so far, a ratio-of-differences quantity (close minus session low, over session range) used to judge trade strength.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (monitoring/context test)

complexity.reason: needs running session high/low accessors

notes: Grimes presents this as a monitoring/visualization tool (a text graph), not explicitly a trade trigger, but the underlying quantity is a legitimate bar-level ratio test; on a daily bar this degenerates to CloseRangePosition since the session equals the bar.

candidates.name: OpenInSessionRangeExtremeDecile
candidates.quote: Calculate the open as percent of day's range = [(open - day's low)/day's range] x 100
candidates.description: Same construction as G08-26 but measuring the session's open location within the session's range instead of the close.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (monitoring/context test)

complexity.reason: needs running session high/low accessors

notes: Minor variant of G08-26; Grimes describes this only as one step of the same text-graph tool, not as an independent signal.

candidates.name: ReenterToFullSizeAfterPullbackToEntryPostPartial
candidates.quote: consider a trader who gets into a trade, takes half of it off at a 1X profit ... and then finds the trade back at the entry price. This trader can add the half she already exited back to the trade
candidates.description: After partial profits were taken at 1x risk, if price pulls back to the original entry price while the remaining position is still open, add back the exited portion at the entry price.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() != 0 and partialProfitTaken == true and close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() and close[0] >= ctx.EntryPrice() - reentryTolerance
candidates.book_order_type: limit re-entry at the entry price

complexity.reason: requires tracking whether a partial exit already occurred on this position, a state the single-net-position engine model may not expose cleanly

notes: Depends on partial-exit bookkeeping (a partialProfitTaken flag) that is not a standard ctx accessor; the authoring pass needs to decide whether the generator's position model can represent this at all.

candidates.name: VolatilitySpikeStdDevOfDailyChange
candidates.quote: my volatility spike indicator, which simply expresses the current day's change (last print to previous day's close) as a standard deviation of the past 20 trading days ... color codes any move larger than three standard deviations up or down
candidates.description: Flags when the current bar's change from the prior close is an unusually large multiple of the standard deviation of daily changes over the past N bars.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - close[1]) >= sdMultiple * stddev(close[0] - close[1], lookback)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (monitoring/context test)

complexity.reason: needs a standard deviation of a bar-to-bar difference series over a rolling window

notes: Grimes originally uses this across a whole watchlist of other markets to color-code a screen; the single-symbol core calculation is what is mineable here, the cross-market screen itself is rejected.

rejected.quote: Trader A finds that a combination of a rather wide stop and a fairly tight profit target works for him ... Trader B ... prefers to have a few large winners
rejected.reason: illustrative narrative about trader psychology and system design trade-offs, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: simply get into a position and give it 10 percent or 20 percent price movement against you ... using the same fixed percentage across different markets is not optimal
rejected.reason: percent-of-price stop threshold, fails the shift test (arbitrary price level)

rejected.quote: Psychological studies have shown that people performing a task with a random reward falsely attribute more of their results to their skill if they have more chances to interact with the process
Once you have determined the size to trade, you have the choice of entering the position all at once or in several pieces
rejected.reason: position sizing / discretionary entry-sizing choice, not a bar-level condition

rejected.quote: Another possibility is to take partial losses as the trade moves against you to reduce the size of the final loss if the trade hits your stop point
rejected.reason: position sizing discussion with no defined bar-level trigger for when to take the partial loss

rejected.quote: Never Add to an Existing Trade ... Add Back Only After Partial Exits ... Add Without Taking Partial Exits ... classic pyramiding plans
rejected.reason: position sizing / pyramiding policy, not a bar-level rule (the one exception with a concrete trigger is mined separately as G08-28)

rejected.quote: I actually have a trading rule that says a stop can never be moved in the direction of risk ... When the decision to tighten the stop was clearly an error, I will move the stop back out
rejected.reason: discretionary discipline policy and a subjective error-correction exception, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: perhaps you are buying into a decline and then some news hits the market that causes ranges to expand ... it may make sense to not complete your buying program, but to move the stop further away
rejected.reason: position sizing / discretionary reaction to a news event, not bar-level data

rejected.quote: Correlated Positions ... Risk no more than 2X to 3X in highly correlated positions ... Maximum Portfolio Risk
rejected.reason: data the engine cannot have: cross-symbol / cross-sector correlation and portfolio-level exposure

rejected.quote: Newer traders should also be wary of trying to do too much at once and of trying to trade too many markets
Position/Risk Sheet ... DateIn, Patt, Ticker, L/S, #, PriceIn, Close, OpenPL, ClosedPL, TotalPL, PL%R, Stop, Risk, PLStop, 1StDev
rejected.reason: manual bookkeeping/accounting fields for a trading journal, not a trading condition

rejected.quote: Dynamic Tracking Tools ... markets in which you have positions and every other significant market ... major broad market indexes ... broad sector indexes
rejected.reason: multi-market watchlist infrastructure; data the engine cannot have (other symbols)

rejected.quote: Practical Tips on Execution ... be careful with market orders ... marketable limit orders should almost always be used
rejected.reason: order-execution / microstructure detail; the engine models fills at open/close, not order-book mechanics

rejected.quote: Executing large orders in thin markets can be challenging ... place a hidden order at 10.02 to 10.05 and see if you are filled there
rejected.reason: order-book / liquidity data the engine cannot have

rejected.quote: Everyone makes mistakes ... the answer is simple: fix the mistake immediately
rejected.reason: pure discretion / operational procedure, no bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 8 is the exit-and-management chapter: initial stop placement (ATR multiples, swing pivots, consolidation extremes), profit targets (risk multiples with partial exits, market-structure/swing-pivot targets), trailing-stop families (moving averages, trend lines, Parabolic SAR, LeBeau's chandelier, price-action stops on closes or fixed lookbacks), breakeven/tightening rules keyed to risk multiples, time stops (hard exit and progressive tightening), gap-through-stop management, and a volatility-spike / session-range-position monitoring tool that reduces to a legitimate bar-level ratio. Position sizing, pyramiding, portfolio/correlation risk, bookkeeping sheets, and execution microstructure were rejected as out of scope for a single-symbol bar-level engine. Every risk-multiple candidate leans on a stopDistance parameter as a stand-in for the entry-side initial risk, since the engine has no accessor for it.
